one_liner: Rust SIMD library and CLI that finds all k-edit occurrences of short DNA/ASCII patterns in long texts, 4-15x faster than Edlib.
what_it_does: Approximate string matching in the Navarro sense: given a pattern (best up to about 1000 characters), a text and a maximum edit distance k, it returns every match end position (search returns only the rightmost position of each local cost minimum, search_all returns all of them) with start, cost and a CIGAR traceback. It supports case-insensitive ASCII, ACGT DNA and IUPAC alphabets, optional reverse-complement search and 'overhang' matches that run off the text ends. It is not a drop-in for Edlib's edlibAlign: the API is a stateful Searcher (Searcher::<Iupac>::new_fwd().search(pattern, text, k)), plus batch variants (search_patterns, search_texts, search_many, and the Sassy2 encode_patterns/search_encoded_patterns path for many equal-length patterns up to 64 bp), a grep/search/filter/crispr CLI, Python (sassy-rs), C (cbindgen header behind the c feature) and third-party DuckDB/R bindings.
how_it_is_fast: Myers-style bit-parallel edit-distance DP with the bit-vectors laid along the text rather than the pattern: each u64 lane holds the horizontal deltas of 64 text columns and the kernel walks the pattern rows, so the work per row is a few SIMD bit operations for 64 text characters. Sassy1 splits one text into 4 overlapping chunks (overlap = ceil((m+k)/64) blocks) and runs one chunk per lane of a 256-bit AVX2 or NEON vector (u64x8 when the target has AVX-512), with an early-termination check once every row exceeds k. Sassy2 instead packs the deltas in the pattern direction, one short pattern per lane, after a suffix filter, which is why it wins on many short patterns over short texts. Edlib, the baseline, runs scalar 64-bit Myers/Hyyro blocks along the pattern with Ukkonen banding, so the gain is algorithmic layout plus SIMD width, not a Rust-versus-C++ effect.
when_to_use: Finding every approximate occurrence (k edits) of 20-1000 bp primers, barcodes, adapters or guides in reads or a genome, where Edlib's HW mode would only report the optimal-cost end positions.
Single-pattern scans over long texts on x86-64 with AVX2/AVX-512 or on ARM with NEON, built with target-cpu=native or x86-64-v3; the committed evals show 0.3-1.9 GB/s per core on 100 kbp texts.

Many equal-length patterns of at most 64 bp against short reads (demultiplexing, barcode lookup): the Sassy2 encoded-pattern path is documented as 10-20x faster than per-pattern search for texts up to 200 bp.
CRISPR off-target search over a whole genome without building an index (sassy crispr, exact PAM by default).
Fuzzy grep over plain ASCII files from the command line (sassy agrep, sassy grep with coloured alignments).
when_not_to_use: Global (end-to-end) or long-read alignment of two long sequences: it is tuned for patterns up to about 1000 and long-query handling is still an open issue (#18); use Edlib NW mode or A*PA2 instead.

Affine-gap or substitution-matrix scoring: it is unit-cost edit distance only, and its greedy traceback (matches, then substitutions, then deletions, then insertions) does not guarantee the fewest substitutions.

Targets without AVX2 or NEON or portable binaries built for baseline x86-64: the crate refuses to build without the SIMD target features unless the slower scalar feature is enabled, so a default cargo build of a dependent crate can fail or be slow.
Searching many patterns against an indexed reference repeatedly: index-based tools (CHOPOFF in the project's own CRISPR test) are slightly faster once the index exists.
IUPAC mode on N-rich data without a cap: every pattern matches NNN...N and a traceback runs from each position in N stretches unless max_n_frac or without_trace is set.

integration.form: crate (rlib and cdylib); also CLI binary, PyPI wheel sassy-rs, bioconda package, C header via the c feature
integration.dependencies: wide (author's git fork), ensure_simd, rayon, itertools, memchr, arrayvec, pa-types, prefetch-index, log, either, derivative; optional clap, needletail, colored, env_logger, num_cpus (cli), rand (diagnostics), pyo3 (python)
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 required at compile time (AVX-512 used when the target enables it), aarch64 with NEON; other targets only with the slower scalar feature
integration.thread_safety: Searcher keeps per-search scratch buffers and its methods take &mut self, so use one Searcher per thread; search_many parallelises over pattern/text pairs with rayon (num_threads 0 reuses the global pool).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: it covers the Edlib HW (infix) use case with a different API and different output semantics (all rightmost local minima with cost <= k, not only optimal-cost ends); there is no NW/SHW global mode and no Edlib-compatible C API.

gotchas: Harness detail behind the 4-15x: evals/src/benchsuite/bench.rs times single-threaded median runs (min 0.1 s, no warmup) on random ACGT data in IUPAC mode for both tools. The committed CSVs report 0 matches in 48 of 49 rows, so the headline measures pure scanning; traceback cost is benchmarked separately (trace.rs). Edlib runs HW mode with EDLIB_TASK_PATH, which returns only the end positions of optimal cost plus one path, while Sassy must report every rightmost local minimum with cost <= k and a CIGAR, so the requested output does not favour Sassy.

Optimisation levels are not matched: Edlib is built through edlib-rs's build.rs by the cmake crate, which maps sassy's release profile (opt-level 3, debug = true) to CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo (-O2 -g) with generic x86-64 flags; the '-D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release' in edlib-rs is passed as a C compiler flag only, so it never reaches the C++ Edlib build. Sassy gets opt-level 3 plus target-cpu=native. Edlib is scalar 64-bit code, so this probably costs it far less than the 4-15x gap.

The '100x faster than SWOffinder' CRISPR figure is against a Java tool (javac-built, run with java) and CHOPOFF is Julia, so neither is a C/C++ baseline; the fork's committed summary.txt contains no Sassy rows (it still lists the CRISPRitz and cas-offinder runs the README says were removed), and the Snakefile builds Sassy from unpinned git HEAD.

Before 0.1.10 (2025-12-10) the sassy grep CLI skipped a record after every 1 MB of input, searching only every other record of a human genome; the library calls behind the Edlib evals were not affected. The current code also auto-selects 8-lane AVX-512 for Sassy1 when target-cpu=native finds avx512f (changelog #68, while Cargo.toml still says the avx512 feature is 'not faster'), so re-runs on AVX-512 machines measure a different kernel than the paper's W=256.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Sassy over A*PA2 (same author) when you search a short pattern inside a long text with up to k edits rather than aligning two whole sequences end to end; pick it over the regex crate, grep clones or needletail when you need edit-distance (fuzzy) matches rather than exact or regex matches.
verified_claims_summary: Committed eval output evals/src/sassy1/output/search_throughput_pat_len.csv (single thread, 100 random patterns x 10 random 100 kbp texts, IUPAC mode) gives Sassy1 0.32-1.87 GB/s against Edlib (C++, via edlib-rs, built RelWithDebInfo) 0.077-0.128 GB/s, i.e. 4.1x (m=1000, k=50) to 14.7x (m=20-50, k=1) (derived from page data), matching the Bioinformatics abstract's 4-15x and 'up to 2 Gbp/s'; the text-length sweep (m=100) gives 4.4-9.3x, lowest for 100-250 bp texts. CPU model is not stated anywhere in the repo; the paper (Bioinformatics, May 2026) was not reachable.
status_note: Actively maintained (825 commits, last commit 2026-09-27, crate 0.2.6 from July 2026, 6106 crates.io downloads), MIT-licensed, published in Bioinformatics and packaged on crates.io, PyPI and bioconda, so it is production-usable for x86-64 AVX2/AVX-512 and NEON targets.
